entries.694815c981b1ccd7366cad43406ced2eaa4587b0: <div sID="gen6449" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="2Sam.23" sID="2Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen6449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6450" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6451" type="x-p"/> The historian is now drawing towards a conclusion of David's reign, and therefore gives us an account here, I. Of some of his last words, which he spoke by inspiration, and which seem to have reference to his seed that was to be for evermore, spoken of in the close of the foregoing chapter, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. Of the great men, especially the military men, that were employed under him, the first three (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.17">ver. 8-17</reference>), two of the next three (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18-2Sam.23.23">ver. 18-23</reference>), and then the thirty, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.24-2Sam.23.39">ver. 24-39</reference>.
entries.8082ba988bb9f12a84876981262ce67b02358594: <div eID="gen6451" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6450" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Last Words. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen6452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now these <hi type="italic">be</hi> the last words of David. David the son of Jesse said, and the man <hi type="italic">who was</hi> raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel, said, <hi type="super">2</hi> The Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake by me, and his word <hi type="italic">was</hi> in my tongue. <hi type="super">3</hi> The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me, He that ruleth over men <hi type="italic">must be</hi> just, ruling in the fear of God. <hi type="super">4</hi> And <hi type="italic">he shall be</hi> as the light of the morning, <hi type="italic">when</hi> the sun riseth, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a morning without clouds; <hi type="italic">as</hi> the tender grass <hi type="italic">springing</hi> out of the earth by clear shining after rain. <hi type="super">5</hi> Although my house <hi type="italic">be</hi> not so with God; yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all <hi type="italic">things,</hi> and sure: for <hi type="italic">this is</hi> all my salvation, and all <hi type="italic">my</hi> desire, although he make <hi type="italic">it</hi> not to grow. <hi type="super">6</hi> But <hi type="italic">the sons</hi> of Belial <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> all of them as thorns thrust away, because they cannot be taken with hands: <hi type="super">7</hi> But the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall touch them must be fenced with iron and the staff of a spear; and they shall be utterly burned with fire in the <hi type="italic">same</hi> place. <div eID="gen6452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6453" type="x-p"/> We have here the last will and testament of king David, or a codicil annexed to it, after he had settled the crown upon Solomon and his treasures upon the temple which was to be built. The last words of great and good men are thought worthy to be in a special manner remarked and remembered. David would have those taken notice of, and added either to his Psalms (as they are here to that in the foregoing chapter) or to the chronicles of his reign. Those words especially in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">v. 5</reference>, though recorded before, we may suppose he often repeated for his own consolation, even to his last breath, and therefore they are called his <hi type="italic">last words.</hi> When we find death approaching we should endeavor both to honour God and to edify those about us with our last words. Let those that have had long experience of God's goodness and the pleasantness of wisdom, when they come to finish their course, leave a record of that experience and bear their testimony to the truth of the promise. We have upon record the last words of Jacob and Moses, and here of David, designed, as those, for a legacy to those that were left behind. We are here told, <div eID="gen6453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6454" type="x-p"/> I. Whose last will and testament this is. This is related either, or is usual, by the testator himself, or rather, by the historian, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">v. 1</reference>. He is described, 1. By the meanness of his original: He was <hi type="italic">the son of Jesse.</hi> It is good for those who are advanced to be corner-stones and top-stones to be reminded, and often to remind themselves, of <hi type="italic">the rock out of which they were hewn.</hi> 2. The height of his elevation: He <hi type="italic">was raised up on high,</hi> as one favoured of God, and designed for something great, raised up as a prince, to sit higher than his neighbours, and as a prophet, to see further; for, (1.) He was <hi type="italic">the anointed of the God of Jacob,</hi> and so was serviceable to the people of God in their civil interests, the protection of their country and the administration of justice among them. (2.) He was <hi type="italic">the sweet psalmist of Israel,</hi> and so was serviceable to them in their religious exercises. He penned the psalms, set the tunes, appointed both the singers and the instruments of music, by which the devotions of good people were much excited and enlarged. Note, The singing of psalms is a sweet ordinance, very agreeable to those that delight in praising God. It is reckoned among the honours to which David was raised up that he was a psalmist: in that he was as truly great as in his being <hi type="italic">the anointed of the God of Jacob.</hi> Note, It is true preferment to be serviceable to the church in acts of devotion and instrumental to promote the blessed work of prayer and praise. Observe, Was David a prince? He was so for Jacob. Was he a psalmist? He was so for Israel. Note, the dispensation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal, and therefore, <hi type="italic">as every man has received the gift, so let him minister the same.</hi> <div eID="gen6454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6455" type="x-p"/> II. What the purport of it is. It is an account of his communion with God. Observe, <div eID="gen6455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6456" type="x-p"/> 1. What God said to him both for his direction and for his encouragement as a king, and to be in like manner, of use to his successors. Pious persons take a pleasure in calling to mind what they have heard from God, in recollecting his word, and revolving it in their minds. Thus what God spoke once David heard twice, yea often. See here, <div eID="gen6456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6457" type="x-p"/> (1.) Who spoke: <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord, the God of Israel,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Rock of Israel,</hi> which some think is an intimation of the Trinity of persons in the Godhead—the Father <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> the Son <hi type="italic">the Rock of Israel,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Spirit</hi> proceeding from the Father and the Son, <hi type="italic">who spoke by the prophets,</hi> and particularly by David, and whose word was not only in his heart, but in his tongue for the benefit of others. David here avows his divine inspiration, that in his psalms, and in this composition, <hi type="italic">The Spirit of God spoke by him.</hi> He, and other holy men, spoke and <hi type="italic">wrote as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.</hi> This puts an honour upon the book of Psalms, and recommends them to our use in our devotions, that they are words which the Holy Ghost teaches. <div eID="gen6457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6458" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was spoken. Here seems to be a distinction made between what the Spirit of God spoke <hi type="italic">by</hi> David, which includes all his psalms, and what the Rock of Israel spoke <hi type="italic">to</hi> David, which concerned himself and his family. Let ministers observe that those by whom God speaks to others are concerned to hear and heed what he speaks to themselves. Those whose office it is to teach others their duty must be sure to learn and do their own. Now that which is here said (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3-2Sam.23.4">v. 3, 4</reference>) may be considered, [1.] With application to David, and his royal family. And so here is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The duty of magistrates enjoined them. When a king was spoken to from God he was not to be complimented with the height of his dignity and the extent of his power, but to be told his duty. "Must is for the king," we say. Here is a <hi type="italic">must</hi> for the king: <hi type="italic">He must be just, ruling in the fear of God;</hi> and so must all inferior magistrates in their places. Let rulers remember that they rule over men—not over beasts which they may enslave and abuse at pleasure, but over reasonable creatures and of the same rank with themselves. They rule over men that have their follies and infirmities, and therefore must be borne with. They rule over men, but under God, and for him; and therefore, 1. They must be just, both to those over whom they rule, in allowing them their rights and properties, and between those over whom they rule, using their power to right the injured against the injurious; see <reference osisRef="Deut.1.16-Deut.1.17">Deut. i. 16, 17</reference>. It is not enough that they do no wrong, but they must not suffer wrong to be done. 2. They must rule in the fear of God, that is, they must themselves be possessed with a fear of God, by which they will be effectually restrained from all acts of injustice and oppression. Nehemiah was so (<reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh. v. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">So did not I, because of the fear of God</hi>), and Joseph, <reference osisRef="Gen.43.18">Gen. xliii. 18</reference>. They must also endeavor to promote the fear of God (that is, the practice of religion) among those over whom they rule. The magistrate is to be the keeper of both tables, and to protect both godliness and honesty. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Prosperity promised them if they do, this duty. <hi type="italic">He that</hi> rules <hi type="italic">in the fear of God shall be as the light of the morning,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">v. 4</reference>. Light is sweet and pleasant, and he that does his duty shall have the comfort of it; his rejoicing will be the testimony of his conscience. Light is bright, and a good prince is illustrious; his justice and piety will be his honour. Light is a blessing, nor are there any greater and more extensive blessings to the public than princes that <hi type="italic">rule in the fear of God.</hi> As <hi type="italic">the light of the morning,</hi> which is most welcome after the darkness of the night (so was David's government after Saul's, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Ps. lxxv. 3</reference>), which is increasing, shines more and more to the perfect day, such is the growing lustre of a good government. It is likewise compared to the tender grass, which the earth produces for the service of man; it brings with it a harvest of blessings. See <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Ps. lxxii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.16">16</reference>, which were also some of the last words of David, and seem to refer to those recorded here. [2.] With application to Christ, the Son of David, and then it must all be taken as a prophecy, and the original will bear it: <hi type="italic">There shall be a rule among men,</hi> or over men, that <hi type="italic">shall be just,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shall rule in the fear of God,</hi> that is, shall order the affairs of religion and divine worship according to his Father's will; and he shall be as <hi type="italic">the light to the morning,</hi> &c., for he is the light of the world, and <hi type="italic">as the tender grass,</hi> for he is the <hi type="italic">branch of the Lord,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">fruit of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.5">Isa. xi. 1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1-Isa.32.2">xxxii. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Ps. lxxii. 2</reference>. God, by the Spirit, gave David the foresight of this, to comfort him under the many calamities of his family and the melancholy prospects he had of the degeneracy of his seed. <div eID="gen6458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6459" type="x-p"/> 2. What comfortable use he made of this which God spoke to him, and what were his devout meditations on it, by way of reply, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">v. 5</reference>. It is not unlike his meditation on occasion of such a message, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.29">2 Sam. vii. 18</reference>, &c. That which goes before the Rock of Israel spoke <hi type="italic">to</hi> him; this the Spirit of God spoke <hi type="italic">by</hi> him, and it is a most excellent confession of his faith and hope in the everlasting covenant. Here is, <div eID="gen6459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6460" type="x-p"/> (1.) Trouble supposed: <hi type="italic">Although my house be not so with God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">although he make it not to grow.</hi> David's family was not so with God as is described (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3-2Sam.23.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), and as he could wish, not so good, not so happy; it had not been so while he lived; he foresaw it would not be so when he was gone, that his house would be neither so pious nor so prosperous as one might have expected the offspring of such a father to be. [1.] <hi type="italic">Not so with God.</hi> Note, We and ours are that really which we are with God. This was what David's heart was upon concerning his children, that they might be right with God, faithful to him and zealous for him. But the children of godly parents are often neither so holy nor so happy as might be expected. We must be made to know that it is corruption, not grace, that runs in the blood, that the race is not to the swift, but that God gives his Spirit as a free-agent. [2.] <hi type="italic">Not made to grow,</hi> in number, in power; it is God that makes families to grow or not to grow, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.41">Ps. cvii. 41</reference>. Good men have often the melancholy prospect of a declining family. David's house was typical of the church of Christ, which is his house, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.3">Heb. iii. 3</reference>. Suppose this be not so with God as we could wish, suppose it be diminished, distressed, disgraced, and weakened, by errors and corruptions, yea, almost extinct, yet God has made a covenant with the church's head, the Son of David, that he will preserve to him a seed, that the gates of hell shall never prevail against his house. This our Saviour comforted himself with in his sufferings, that the covenant with him stood firm, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 10-12</reference>. (2.) Comfort ensured: <hi type="italic">Yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant.</hi> Whatever trouble a child of God may have the prospect of, still he has some comfort or other to balance it with (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.9">2 Cor. iv. 8, 9</reference>), and there is none like this of the Psalmist, which may be understood, [1.] Of the covenant of royalty (in the type) which God made with David and his seed, touching the kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.11-Ps.132.12">Ps. cxxxii. 11, 12</reference>. But, [2.] It must look further, to the covenant of grace made with all believers, that God will be, in Christ, to them a God, which was signified by the covenant of royalty, and therefore the promises of the covenant are called <hi type="italic">the sure mercies of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>. It is this only that is the everlasting covenant, and it cannot be imagined that David, who, in so many of his psalms, speaks so clearly concerning Christ and the grace of the gospel, should forget it in his last words. God has made a covenant of grace with us in Jesus Christ, and we are here told, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it is an <hi type="italic">everlasting</hi> covenant, from everlasting in the contrivance and counsel of it, and to everlasting in the continuance and consequences of it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it is <hi type="italic">ordered,</hi> well ordered in all things, admirably well, to advance the glory of God and the honour of the Mediator, together with the holiness and comfort of believers. It is herein well ordered, that whatever is required in the covenant is promised, and that every transgression in the covenant does not throw us out of covenant, and that it puts our salvation, not in our own keeping, but in the keeping of a Mediator. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That it is <hi type="italic">sure,</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> sure because well ordered; the general offer of it is sure; the promised mercies are sure on the performance of the conditions. The particular application of it to true believers is sure; it is sure to all the seed. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That it is <hi type="italic">all our salvation.</hi> Nothing but this will save us, and this is sufficient: it is this only upon which our salvation depends. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> That therefore it must be <hi type="italic">all our desire.</hi> Let me have an interest in this covenant and the promises of it, and I have enough, I desire no more. <div eID="gen6460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6461" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is the doom of the sons of Belial read, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6-2Sam.23.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. (1.) They shall be thrust away as thorns—rejected, abandoned. They are like thorns, not to be touched with hands, so passionate and furious that they cannot be managed or dealt with by a wise and faithful reproof, but must be restrained by law and the sword of justice (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Ps. xxxii. 9</reference>); and therefore, like thorns, (2.) They shall, at length, be utterly burnt with fire in the same place, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.8">Heb. vi. 8</reference>. Now this is intended, [1.] As a direction to magistrates to use their power for the punishing and suppressing of wickedness. Let them <hi type="italic">thrust away the sons of Belial;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">Ps. ci. 8</reference>. Or, [2.] As a caution to magistrates, and particularly to David's sons and successors, to see that they be not themselves sons of Belial (as too many of them were), for then neither the dignity of their place nor their relation to David would secure them from being thrust away by the righteous judgments of God. Though men could not deal with them, God would. Or, [3.] As a prediction of the ruin of all the implacable enemies of Christ's kingdom. There are enemies without, that openly oppose it and fight against it, and enemies within, that secretly betray it and are false to it; both are sons of Belial, children of the wicked one, of the serpent's seed; both are as thorns, grievous and vexatious: but both shall be so thrust away as that Christ will set up his kingdom in despite of their enmity, will <hi type="italic">go through them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa. xxvii. 4</reference>), and will, in due time, bless his church with such peace that there shall be <hi type="italic">no pricking brier nor grieving thorn.</hi> And those that will not repent, to give glory to God, shall, in the judgment-day (to which the Chaldee paraphrast refers this), be burnt with unquenchable fire. See <reference osisRef="Luke.19.27">Luke xix. 27</reference>.
entries.10d9e70285c6b6fef9628f280f83da073e2f9589: <div eID="gen6461" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Mighty Men. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1054.)</title> <div sID="gen6462" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> These <hi type="italic">be</hi> the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains; the same <hi type="italic">was</hi> Adino the Eznite: <hi type="italic">he lift up his spear</hi> against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time. <hi type="super">9</hi> And after him <hi type="italic">was</hi> Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite, <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines <hi type="italic">that</hi> were there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel were gone away: <hi type="super">10</hi> He arose, and smote the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clave unto the sword: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> wrought a great victory that day; and the people returned after him only to spoil. <hi type="super">11</hi> And after him <hi type="italic">was</hi> Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite. And the Philistines were gathered together into a troop, where was a piece of ground full of lentiles: and the people fled from the Philistines. <hi type="super">12</hi> But he stood in the midst of the ground, and defended it, and slew the Philistines: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> wrought a great victory. <hi type="super">13</hi> And three of the thirty chief went down, and came to David in the harvest time unto the cave of Adullam: and the troop of the Philistines pitched in the valley of Rephaim. <hi type="super">14</hi> And David <hi type="italic">was</hi> then in a hold, and the garrison of the Philistines <hi type="italic">was</hi> then <hi type="italic">in</hi> Bethlehem. <hi type="super">15</hi> And David longed, and said, Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Bethlehem, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the gate! <hi type="super">16</hi> And the three mighty men brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> by the gate, and took <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and brought <hi type="italic">it</hi> to David: nevertheless he would not drink thereof, but poured it out unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said, Be it far from me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , that I should do this: <hi type="italic">is not this</hi> the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives? therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mighty men. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief among three. And he lifted up his spear against three hundred, <hi type="italic">and</hi> slew <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and had the name among three. <hi type="super">19</hi> Was he not most honourable of three? therefore he was their captain: howbeit he attained not unto the <hi type="italic">first</hi> three. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel, who had done many acts, he slew two lionlike men of Moab: he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow: <hi type="super">21</hi> And he slew an Egyptian, a goodly man: and the Egyptian had a spear in his hand; but he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian's hand, and slew him with his own spear. <hi type="super">22</hi> These <hi type="italic">things</hi> did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among three mighty men. <hi type="super">23</hi> He was more honourable than the thirty, but he attained not to the <hi type="italic">first</hi> three. And David set him over his guard. <hi type="super">24</hi> Asahel the brother of Joab <hi type="italic">was</hi> one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, <hi type="super">25</hi> Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite, <hi type="super">26</hi> Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, <hi type="super">27</hi> Abiezer the Anethothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite, <hi type="super">28</hi> Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite, <hi type="super">29</hi> Heleb the son of Baanah, a Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai out of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin, <hi type="super">30</hi> Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash, <hi type="super">31</hi> Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite, <hi type="super">32</hi> Eliahba the Shaalbonite, of the sons of Jashen, Jonathan, <hi type="super">33</hi> Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite, <hi type="super">34</hi> Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, <hi type="super">35</hi> Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite, <hi type="super">36</hi> Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite, <hi type="super">37</hi> Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armourbearer to Joab the son of Zeruiah, <hi type="super">38</hi> Ira an Ithrite, Gareb an Ithrite, <hi type="super">39</hi> Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all. <div eID="gen6462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6463" type="x-p"/> I. The catalogue which the historian has here left upon record of the great soldiers that were in David's time is intended, 1. For the honour of David, who trained them up in the arts of exercises of war, and set them an example of conduct and courage. It is the reputation as well as the advantage of a prince to be attended and served by such brave men as are here described. 2. For the honour of those worthies themselves, who were instrumental to bring David to the crown, settle and protect him in the throne, and enlarge his conquests. Note, Those that in public stations venture themselves, and lay out themselves, to serve the interests of their country, are worthy of double honour, both to be respected by those of their own age and to be remembered by posterity. 3. To excite those that come after to a generous emulation. 4. To show how much religion contributes to the inspiring of men with true courage. David, both by his psalms and by his offerings for the service of the temple, greatly promoted piety among the grandees of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.6">1 Chron. xxix. 6</reference>), and, when they became famous for piety, they became famous for bravery. <div eID="gen6463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6464" type="x-p"/> II. Now these mighty men are here divided into three ranks:— <div eID="gen6464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6465" type="x-p"/> 1. The first three, who had done the greatest exploits and thereby gained the greatest reputation—Adino (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">v. 8</reference>), Eleazar (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.9-2Sam.23.10">v. 9, 10</reference>), and Shammah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.11-2Sam.23.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. I do not remember that we read of any of these, or of their actions, any where in all the story of David but here and in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11-1Chr.11.47">1 Chron. xi</reference>. Many great and remarkable events are passed by in the annals, which relate rather the blemishes than the glories of David's reign, especially after his sin in the matter Uriah; so that we may conclude his reign to have been really more illustrious than it has appeared to us while reading the records of it. The exploits of this brave triumvirate are here recorded. They signalized themselves in the wars of Israel against their enemies, especially the Philistines. (1.) Adino slew 800 at once with his spear. (2.) Eleazar defied the Philistines, as they by Goliath, had defied Israel, but with better success and greater bravery; for when the men of Israel had gone away, he not only kept his ground, but <hi type="italic">arose, and smote the Philistines,</hi> on whom God struck a terror equal to the courage with which this great hero was inspired. His hand was weary, and yet it clave to his sword; as long as he had any strength remaining he held his weapon and followed his blow. Thus, in the service of God, we should keep up the willingness and resolution of the spirit, notwithstanding the weakness and weariness of the flesh—faint, yet pursuing (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.4">Judg. viii. 4</reference>), the hand weary, yet not quitting the sword. Now that Eleazar had beaten the enemy, the men of Israel, who had gone away from the battle (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.9">v. 9</reference>), returned to spoil, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.10">v. 10</reference>. It is common for those who quit the field, when any thing is to be done to hasten to it when any thing is to be gotten. (3.) Shammah met with a party of the enemy, that were foraging, and routed them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.11-2Sam.23.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. But observe, both concerning this exploit and the former, it is here said, <hi type="italic">The Lord wrought a great victory.</hi> Note, How great soever the bravery of the instruments is, the praise of the achievement must be given to God. These fought the battles, but God wrought the victory. Let not the strong man then glory in his strength, nor in any of his military operations, but <hi type="italic">let him that glories glory in the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen6465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6466" type="x-p"/> 2. The next three were distinguished from, and dignified above, the thirty, but attained not to the first three, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">v. 23</reference>. All great men are not of the same size. Many a bright and benign star there is which is not of the first magnitude, and many a good ship not of the first rate. Of this second triumvirate two only are named, Abishai and Benaiah, whom we have often met with in the story of David, and who seem to have been not inferior in serviceableness, though they were in dignity, to the first three. Here is, <div eID="gen6466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6467" type="x-p"/> (1.) A brave action of these three in conjunction. They attended David in his troubles, when he absconded, in the cave of Adullam (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">v. 13</reference>), suffered with him, and therefore were afterwards preferred by him. When David and his brave men who attended him, who had acted so vigorously against the Philistines, were, by the iniquity of the times, in Saul's reign, driven to shelter themselves from his rage in caves and strong holds, no marvel that the Philistines pitched in the valley of Rephaim, and put a garrison even in Bethlehem itself, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13-2Sam.23.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. If the church's guides are so misled as to persecute some of her best friends and champions, the common enemy will, no doubt, get advantage by it. If David had had his liberty, Bethlehem would not have been now in the Philistines' hands. But, being so, we are here told, [1.] How earnestly David longed for the water of the well of Bethlehem. Some make it a public-spirited wish, and that he meant, "O that we could drive the garrison of the Philistines out of Bethlehem, and make that beloved city of mine our own again!" the well being put for the city, as the river often signifies the country it passes through. But if he meant so, those about him did not understand him; therefore it seems rather to be an instance of his weakness. It was harvest-time; the weather was hot; he was thirsty; perhaps good water was scarce, and therefore he earnestly wished, "O that I could but have one draught of the water of the well of Bethlehem!" With the water of that well he had often refreshed himself when he was a youth, and nothing now will serve him but that, though it is almost impossible to come at it. He strangely indulged a humour which he could give no reason for. Other water might quench his thirst as well, but he had a fancy for that above any. It is folly to entertain such fancies and greater folly to insist upon the gratification of them. We ought to check our appetites when they go out inordinately towards those things that really are more pleasant and grateful than other things (<hi type="italic">Be not desirous of dainties</hi>), much more when they are thus set upon such things as only please a humour. [2.] How bravely his three mighty men, Abishai, Benaiah, and another not named, ventured through the camp of the Philistines, upon the very mouth of danger, and fetched water from the well of Bethlehem, without David's knowledge, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.16">v. 16</reference>. When he wished for it he was far from desiring that any of his men should venture their lives for it; but those three did, to show, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How much they valued their prince, and with what pleasure they could run the greatest hardships in his service. David, though anointed king, was as yet an exile, a poor prince that had no external advantages to recommend him to the affection and esteem of his attendants, nor was he in any capacity to prefer or reward them; yet those three were thus zealous for his satisfaction, firmly believing the time of recompence would come. Let us be willing to venture in the cause of Christ, even when it is a suffering cause, as those who are assured that it will prevail and that we shall not lose by it at last. Were they so forward to expose themselves upon the least hint of their prince's mind and so ambitious to please him? And shall not we covet to approve ourselves to our Lord Jesus by a ready compliance with every intimation of his will given us by his word, Spirit and providence? <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How little they feared the Philistines. They were glad of an occasion to defy them. Whether they broke through the host clandestinely, and with such art that the Philistines did not discover them, or openly, and with such terror in their looks that the Philistines durst not oppose them, is not certain; it should seem, they forced their way, sword in hand. But see, [3.] How self-denyingly David, when he had this far-fetched dear-bought water, <hi type="italic">poured it out before the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.17">v. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Thus he would show the tender regard he had to the lives of his soldiers, and how far he was from being prodigal of their blood, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Ps. lxxii. 14</reference>. In God's sight the death of his saints is precious. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Thus he would testify his sorrow for speaking that foolish word which occasioned those men to put their lives in their hands. Great men should take heed what they say, lest any bad use be made of it by those about them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Thus he would prevent the like rashness in any of his men for the future. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Thus he would cross his own foolish fancy, and punish himself for entertaining and indulging it, and show that he had sober thoughts to correct his rash ones, and knew how to deny himself even in that which he was most fond of. Such generous mortifications become the wise, the great, and the good. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> Thus he would honour God and give glory to him. The water purchased at this rate he thought too precious for his own drinking and fit only to be poured out to God as a drink-offering. If it was the blood of these men, it was God's due, for the blood was always his. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> Bishop Patrick speaks of some who think that David hereby showed that it was not material water he longed for, but the Messiah, who had the water of life, who, he knew, should be born at Bethlehem, which the Philistines therefore should not be able to destroy. <hi type="italic">Seventhly,</hi> Did David look upon that water as very precious which was got at the hazard of these men's blood, and shall not we much more value those benefits for the purchasing of which our blessed Saviour shed his blood? Let us not undervalue the blood of the covenant, as those do that undervalue the blessings of the covenant. <div eID="gen6467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6468" type="x-p"/> (2.) The brave actions of two of them on other occasions. Abishai slew 300 men at once, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18-2Sam.23.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Benaiah did many great things. [1.] He slew two Moabites that were lion-like men, so bold and strong, so fierce and furious. [2.] He slew an Egyptian, on what occasion it is not said; he was well armed but Benaiah attacked him with no other weapon than a walking staff, dexterously wrested his spear out of his hand, and slew him with it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.21">v. 21</reference>. For these and similar exploits David preferred him to be captain of the life-guard or standing forces, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">v. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen6468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6469" type="x-p"/> 3. Inferior to the second three, but of great note, were the thirty-one here mentioned by name, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.24-2Sam.23.39">v. 24</reference>, &c. Asahel is the first, who was slain by Abner in the beginning of David's reign, but lost not his place in this catalogue. Elhanan is the next, brother to Eleazar, one of the first three, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.9">v. 9</reference>. The surnames here given them are taken, as it should seem, from the places of their birth or habitation, as many surnames with us originally were. From all parts of the nation, the most wise and valiant were picked up to serve the king. Several of those who are named we find captains of the twelve courses which David appointed, one for each month in the year, <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.1-1Chr.27.5">1 Chron. xxvii</reference>. Those that did worthily were preferred according to their merits. One of them was the son of Ahithophel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.34">v. 34</reference>), the son famous in the camp as the father at the council-board. But to find Uriah the Hittite bringing up the rear of these worthies, as it revives the remembrance of David's sin, so it aggravates it, that a man who deserved so well of his king and country should be so ill treated. Joab is not mentioned among all these, either, (1.) to be mentioned; the first, of the first three sat chief among the captains, but Joab was over them as general. Or, (2.) Because he was so bad that he did not deserve to be mentioned; for though he was confessedly a great soldier, and one that had so much religion in him as to dedicate of his spoils to the house of God (<reference osisRef="1Chr.21.28">1 Chron. xxvi. 28</reference>), yet he lost as much honour by slaying two of David's friends as ever he got by slaying his enemies. <div eID="gen6469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6470" type="x-p"/> Christ, the Son of David, has his worthies too, who like David's, are influenced by his example, fight his battles against the spiritual enemies of his kingdom, and in his strength are more than conquerors. Christ's apostles were his immediate attendants, did and suffered great things for him, and at length came to reign with him. They are mentioned with honour in the New Testament, as these in the Old, especially, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Rev. xxi. 14</reference>. Nay, all the good soldiers of Jesus Christ have their names better preserved than even these worthies have; for they are written in heaven. This honour have all his saints.  <chapter eID="2Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen6470" type="x-p"/>

entries.20f9e8890dd5b863ddd04050d44d8479a2188c07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3041"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <div sID="gen4214" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.7">2Sa 23:1-7</reference>. David Professes His Faith in God's Promises.<div eID="gen4214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4215" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3041"/><hi type="bold">1. Now these be the last words of David--</hi>Various opinions are entertained as to the precise meaning of this statement, which, it is obvious, proceeded from the compiler or collector of the sacred canon. Some think that, as there is no division of chapters in the Hebrew Scriptures, this introduction was intended to show that what follows is no part of the preceding song. Others regard this as the last of the king's poetical compositions; while still others consider it the last of his utterances as an inspired writer.<div eID="gen4215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raised up on high--</hi>from an obscure family and condition to a throne.<div eID="gen4216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the anointed of the God of Jacob--</hi>chosen to be king by the special appointment of that God, to whom, by virtue of an ancient covenant, the people of Israel owed all their peculiar destiny and distinguished privileges.<div eID="gen4217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sweet psalmist of Israel--</hi>that is, delightful, highly esteemed. <div eID="gen4218" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5f04f3e421bc15e7cde2d4231f1d720b92f6357: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3042"/><div sID="gen4219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3042"/><hi type="bold">2. The Spirit of the Lord spake by me--</hi>Nothing can more clearly show that all that is excellent in spirit, beautiful in language, or grand in prophetic imagery, which the Psalms of David contain, were owing, not to his superiority in natural talents or acquired knowledge, but to the suggestion and dictates of God's Spirit. <div eID="gen4219" type="x-p"/>
entries.da76ba65cbc6d0f2a5c687d326975e3f42b4b353: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3043"/><div sID="gen4220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3043"/><hi type="bold">3. the Rock of Israel--</hi>This metaphor, which is commonly applied by the sacred writers to the Almighty, was very expressive to the minds of the Hebrew people. Their national fortresses, in which they sought security in war, were built on high and inaccessible rocks.<div eID="gen4220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spake to me--</hi>either preceptively, giving the following counsels respecting the character of an upright ruler in Israel, or prophetically, concerning David and his royal dynasty, and the great Messiah, of whom many think this is a prophecy, rendering the words, "he that ruleth"--"there shall be a ruler over men." <div eID="gen4221" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f60e715c97b938cb55faf0c33adbedac824bc9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3044"/><div sID="gen4222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3044"/><hi type="bold">4. as the tender grass springing out of the earth by clear shining after rain--</hi>Little patches of grass are seen rapidly springing up in Palestine after rain; and even where the ground has been long parched and bare, within a few days or hours after the enriching showers begin to fall, the face of the earth is so renewed that it is covered over with a pure fresh mantle of green. <div eID="gen4222" type="x-p"/>
entries.55137e1dd11910f6b08f267bf0457cf4e8dc2e30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3045"/><div sID="gen4223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3045"/><hi type="bold">5. Although my house be not so with God; yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure--</hi>"the light of the morning," that is, the beginning of David's kingdom, was unlike the clear brilliant dawn of an Eastern day but was overcast by many black and threatening clouds; neither he nor his family had been like the tender grass springing up from the ground and flourishing by the united influences of the sun and rain; but rather like the grass that withereth and is prematurely cut down. The meaning is: although David's house had not flourished in an uninterrupted course of worldly prosperity and greatness, according to his hopes; although great crimes and calamities had beclouded his family history; some of the most promising branches of the royal tree had been cut down in his lifetime and many of his successors should suffer in like manner for their personal sins; although many reverses and revolutions may overtake his race and his kingdom, yet it was to him a subject of the highest joy and thankfulness that God will inviolably maintain His covenant with his family, until the advent of his greatest Son, the Messiah, who was the special object of his desire, and the author of his salvation. <div eID="gen4223" type="x-p"/>
entries.30ef8f1270bc694676b59a0b81048c40d9715ede: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3046"/><div sID="gen4224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3046"/><hi type="bold">6. But the sons of Belial shall be all of them as thorns--</hi>that is, the wicked enemies and persecutors of this kingdom of righteousness. They resemble those prickly, thorny plants which are twisted together, whose spires point in every direction, and which are so sharp and strong that they cannot be touched or approached without danger; but hard instruments and violent means must be taken to destroy or uproot them. So God will remove or destroy all who are opposed to this kingdom.<div eID="gen4224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4225" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.39">2Sa 23:8-39</reference>. A Catalogue of His Mighty Men. <div eID="gen4225" type="x-p"/>
entries.0aab83f333b1c77479f0dab648fe341e80566156: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3047"/><div sID="gen4226" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3047"/><hi type="bold">8. These be the names of the mighty men whom David had--</hi>This verse should be translated thus: He who sits in the seat of the Tachmonite (that is, of Jashobeam the Hachmonite), who was chief among the captains, the same is Adino the Eznite; he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time. The text is corrupt in this passage; the number eight hundred should be three hundred [Davidson, Hermeneutics]. Under Joab he was chief or president of the council of war. The first or highest order was composed of him and his two colleagues, Eleazar and Shammah. Eleazar seems to have been left to fight the Philistines alone; and on his achieving the victory, they returned to the spoil. In like manner Shammah was left to stand alone in his glory, when the Lord, by him, wrought a great victory. It is not very easy to determine whether the exploits that are afterwards described were performed by the first or the second three. <div eID="gen4226" type="x-p"/>
entries.72f5ee69187951659bff24f4ed5f7f39b8a609b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3048"/><div sID="gen4227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3048"/><hi type="bold">15-16. the well of Beth-lehem--</hi>An ancient cistern, with four or five holes in the solid rock, at about ten minutes distance to the north of the eastern corner of the hill of Beth-lehem, is pointed out by the natives as Bir-Daoud; that is, David's well. Dr. Robinson doubts the identity of the well; but others think that there are no good grounds for doing so. Certainly, considering this to be the ancient well, Beth-lehem must have once extended ten minutes further to the north, and must have lain in times of old, not as now, on the summit, but on the northern rise of the hill; for the well is by or (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.7">1Ch 11:7</reference>) at the gate. I find in the description of travellers, that the common opinion is, that David's captains had come from the southeast, in order to obtain, at the risk of their lives, the so-much-longed-for water; while it is supposed that David himself was then in the great cave that is not far to the southeast of Beth-lehem; which cave is generally held to have been that of Adullam. But (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>) Adullam lay "in the valley"; that is, in the undulating plain at the western base of the mountains of Judea and consequently to the southwest of Beth-lehem. Be this as it may, David's men had in any case to break through the host of the Philistines, in order to reach the well; and the position of Bir-Daoud agrees well with this [Van De Velde]. <div eID="gen4227" type="x-p"/>
entries.6528460019baae0faa4d9c9cce173baa14f1f947: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3049"/><div sID="gen4228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3049"/><hi type="bold">19-39. the first three--</hi>The mighty men or champions in David's military staff were divided into three classes--the highest, Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah; the second class, Abishai, Benaiah, and Asahel; and the third class, the thirty, of which Asahel was the chief. There are thirty-one mentioned in the list, including Asahel; and these added to the two superior orders make thirty-seven. Two of them, we know, were already dead; namely, Asahel [2Sa 3:30] and Uriah [2Sa 11:17]; and if the dead, at the drawing up of the list, amounted to seven, then we might suppose a legion of honor, consisting of the definite number thirty, where the vacancies, when they occurred, were replaced by fresh appointments. <chapter eID="2Sam.23"/>

entries.8016c80291a566f25f35674a262431ea43a8a271: <div eID="gen11340" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11341" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11342" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11342" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11341" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11343" type="x-p"/> The last words of David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.7">2Sam 23:1-7</reference>. The names and exploits of has thirty-seven worthies, vv. 8-39. <div eID="gen11343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11344" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen11344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11345" type="x-p"/> These be the last words of David - I suppose the last poetical composition is here intended. He might have spoken many words after these in prose, but none in verse. Other meanings are given; this I prefer. <div eID="gen11345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11346" type="x-p"/> The words of this song contain a glorious prediction of the Messiah's kingdom and conquests, in highly poetic language. <div eID="gen11346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11347" type="x-p"/> The sweet psalmist of Israel - This character not only belonged to him as the finest poet in Israel, but as the finest and most Divine poet of the whole Christian world. The sweet psalmist of Israel has been the sweet psalmist of every part of the habitable world, where religion and piety have been held in reverence.
entries.5eeedc73b9f2791fab55f1bfdfa78cb2783accac: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen11347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11348" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of the Lord spake by me - Hence the matter of his writing came by direct and immediate inspiration. <div eID="gen11348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11349" type="x-p"/> His word was in my tongue - Hence the words of this writing were as directly inspired as the matter.
entries.d13cfa844ea1fbdc4f8bd6d74e03d8eec602186e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11350" type="x-p"/> The Rock of Israel - The Fountain whence Israel was derived. <div eID="gen11350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11351" type="x-p"/> He that ruleth over men must be just - More literally, מושל באדם צדיק moshel baadam tsaddik, He that ruleth in man is the just one; or, The just one is the ruler among men. <div eID="gen11351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11352" type="x-p"/> Ruling in the fear of God - It is by God's fear that Jesus Christ rules the hearts of all his followers; and he who has not the fear of God before his eyes, can never be a Christian.
entries.92b424b9500874ce7767b859748d7b7a64ed9312: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen11352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11353" type="x-p"/> He shall be as the light of the morning - This verse is very obscure, for it does not appear from it who the person is of whom the prophet speaks. As the Messiah seems to be the whole subject of these last words of David, he is probably the person intended. One of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. Supplies the word יהוה Yehovah; and he therefore translates, As the light of the morning ariseth Jehovah (see below) He shall be the Sun of righteousness, bringing salvation in his rays, and shining - illuminating the children of men, with increasing splendor, as long as the sun and moon endure. <div eID="gen11353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11354" type="x-p"/> As the tender grass - The effects of this shining, and of the rays of his grace, shall be like the shining of the sun upon the young grass or corn, after a plentiful shower of rain.
entries.e59e21420d6178815fcaf8aeb45432f12fd6d176: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11355" type="x-p"/> Although my house be not so with God - Instead of כן ken, so, read כן kun, established; and let the whole verse be considered as an interrogation, including a positive assertion; and the sense will be at once clear and consistent: "for is not my house (family) established with God; because he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all, and preserved? For this (He) is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he make it (or him) not to spring up." All is sure relative to my spiritual successor, though he do not as yet appear; the covenant is firm, and it will spring forth in due time. See the observations at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.39">2Sam 23:39</reference>note).
entries.9cb8ba8895341537f9c538f4686f25af6514657e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen11355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11356" type="x-p"/> But the sons of Belial shall be all of them as thorns - There is no word in the text for sons; it is simply Belial, the good-for-nothing man, and may here refer - first to Saul, and secondly to the enemies of our Lord. <div eID="gen11356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11357" type="x-p"/> As thorns thrust away - A metaphor taken from hedging; the workman thrusts the thorns aside either with his bill or hand, protected by his impenetrable mitten or glove, till, getting a fair blow at the roots, he cuts them all down. The man is fenced with iron, and the handle of his bill is like the staff of a spear. This is a good representation of the dubbing-bill, with which they slash the thorn hedge on each side before they level the tops by the pruning-shears. The handle is five or six feet long. This is a perfectly natural and intelligible image.
entries.c3d8148953f09b5db12fdd467e8c909ab38ec183: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen11357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11358" type="x-p"/> These be the names of the mighty men - This chapter should be collated with the parallel place, 1 Chronicles 11:11-47; and see Kennicott's First Dissertation on the printed Hebrew text, pages 64-471. <div eID="gen11358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11359" type="x-p"/> The Tachmonite that sat in the seat - Literally and properly, Jashobeam the Hachmonite. See <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Chr 11:11</reference>. <div eID="gen11359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11360" type="x-p"/> The same was Adino the Eznite - This is a corruption for he lift up his spear. See <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Chr 11:11</reference>. <div eID="gen11360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11361" type="x-p"/> Eight hundred, whom he slew at one time - Three hundred is the reading in Chronicles, and seems to be the true one. The word חלל chalal, which we translate slain, should probably be translated soldiers, as in the Septuagint, στρατιωτας; he withstood three hundred Soldiers at one time. See the note on David's lamentation over Saul and Jonathan, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">2Sam 1:21</reference> (note), and Kennicott's First Dissertation, p. 101. Dr. Kennicott observes: "This one verse contains three great corruptions in the Hebrew text: <div eID="gen11361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11362" type="x-p"/> 1. The proper name of the hero Jashobeam is turned into two common words, rendered, that sat in the seat. <div eID="gen11362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11363" type="x-p"/> 2. The words, he lift up his spear, הואעורר את חניתו hu orer eth chanitho, are turned into two proper names wholly inadmissible here: הוא עדינו העצני hu Adino haetsni, he was Adino the Eznite; it being nearly as absurd to say that Jashobeam the Hachmonite was the same with Adino the Eznite, as that David the Beth-lehemite was the same with Elijah the Tishbite. <div eID="gen11363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11364" type="x-p"/> 3. The number eight hundred was probably at first three hundred, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Chr 11:11</reference>." <div eID="gen11364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11365" type="x-p"/> See Kennicott, ubi supr.
entries.49d511b96e32d076a259830586563c5586ccbb54: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen11365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11366" type="x-p"/> When they defied the Philistines that were there gathered - This is supposed to refer to the war in which David slew Goliath.
entries.bdbd9d9bd7e0a4883e99b4e6a0b67a0620dc7914: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11367" type="x-p"/> A piece of ground full of lentiles - In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Chr 11:13</reference> it is a parcel of ground full of barley. There is probably a mistake of עדשים adashim, lentiles, for שעורים seorim, barley, or vice versa. Some think there were both lentiles and barley in the field, and that a marauding party of the Philistines came to destroy or carry them off, and these worthies defeated the whole, and saved the produce of the field. This is not unlikely.
entries.b536b03a62a1265fc283851529b28eef54481fdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen11367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11368" type="x-p"/> And three of the thirty - The word שלשים shalishim, which we translate thirty, probably signifies an office or particular description of men. Of these shalishim we have here thirty-seven, and it can scarcely be said with propriety that we have thirty-seven out of thirty; and besides, in the parallel place, 1 Chronicles 11:11-47, there are sixteen added. The captains over Pharaoh's chariots are termed שלשים shalishim, <reference osisRef="Exo.14.7">Exo 14:7</reference>. <div eID="gen11368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11369" type="x-p"/> The Philistines pitched in the valley of Rephaim - This is the same war which is spoken of <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.17">2Sam 5:17</reference>, etc.
entries.3dcba4e49b980a7691c65e271b6cc9ae5c12e3ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen11369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11370" type="x-p"/> The water of the well of Bethlehem - This was David's city, and he knew the excellence of the water which was there; and being near the place, and parched with thirst, it was natural for him to wish for a draught of water out of that well. These three heroes having heard it, though they received no command from David, broke through a company of the Philistines, and brought away some of the water. When brought to David he refused to drink it: for as the men got it at the hazard of their lives, he considered it as their blood, and gave thereby a noble instance of self-denial. There is no evidence that David had requested them to bring it; they had gone for it of their own accord, and without the knowledge of David.
entries.53b82c308d1a9d64b9d84b1bdaaab52b20ecc57c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen11370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11371" type="x-p"/> Poured it out unto the Lord - To make libations, both of water and wine, was a frequent custom among the heathens. We have an almost similar account in Arrian's Life of Alexander: "When his army was greatly oppressed with heat and thirst, a soldier brought him a cup of water; he ordered it to be carried back, saying, I cannot bear to drink alone while so many are in want, and this cup is too small to be divided among the whole." Tunc poculo pleno sicut oblatum est reddito: Non solus, inquit, bibere sustineo, nec tam exiguum dividere omnibus possum. - Arrian, lib. vi. <div eID="gen11371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11372" type="x-p"/> The example was noble in both cases, but David added piety to bravery; he poured it out unto the Lord.
entries.780d50baaf17a3e6d7924dff74e045c1ccdfab3e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen11372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11373" type="x-p"/> Two lion-like men of Moab - Some think that two real lions are meant; some that they were two savage gigantic men; others, that two fortresses are meant. The words שני אראל מואב sheney ariel Moab may signify, as the Targum has rendered it, ית תרין רברבי מואב yath terein rabrebey Moab, "The two princes of Moab."
entries.d1dd5f0a49f75ee8ee32798ca55c3db38d6e3439: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen11373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11374" type="x-p"/> He slew an Egyptian - This man in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.23">1Chr 11:23</reference> is stated to have been five cubits high, about seven feet six inches. <div eID="gen11374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11375" type="x-p"/> He went down to him with a staff - I have known men who, with a staff only for their defense, could render the sword of the best practiced soldier of no use to him. I have seen even a parallel instance of a man with his staff being attacked by a soldier with his hanger; he soon beat the weapon out of the soldier's hand, and could easily have slain him with his own sword. <div eID="gen11375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11376" type="x-p"/> We have a good elucidation of this in a duel between Dioxippus the Athenian and Horratas a Macedonian, before Alexander: "The Macedonian, proud of his military skill, treated the naked Athenian with contempt, and then challenged him to fight with him the ensuing day. The Macedonian came armed cap-a-pie to the place; on his left arm he had a brazen shield, and in the same hand a spear called sarissa; he had a javelin in his right hand, and a sword girded on his side; in short, he appeared armed as though he were going to contend with a host. Dioxippus came into the field with a chaplet on his head, a purple sash on his left arm, his body naked, smeared over with oil, and in his right hand a strong knotty club, (dextra validum nodosumque stipitem praeferebat). Horratas, supposing he could easily kill his antagonist while at a distance, threw his javelin, which Dioxippus, suddenly stooping, dexterously avoided, and, before Horratas could transfer the spear from his left to his right hand, sprang forward, and with one blow of his club, broke it in two. The Macedonian being deprived of both his spears, began to draw his sword; but before he could draw it out Dioxippus seized him, tripped up his heels, and threw him with great violence on the ground, (pedibus repente subductis arietavit in terram). He then put his foot on his neck, drew out his sword, and lifting up his club, was about to dash out the brains of the overthrown champion, had he not been prevented by the king." - Q. Curt. lib. ix., cap. 7. <div eID="gen11376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11377" type="x-p"/> How similar are the two cases! He went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian's hands, and slew him with his own spear. Benaiah appears to have been just such another clubsman as Dioxippus.
entries.e428d6ab084c06557e7ecda6663998270eafbf96: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen11377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11378" type="x-p"/> David set him over his guard - The Vulgate renders this, Fecitque eun sibi David auricularium a secreto, "David made him his privy counsellor;" or, according to the Hebrew, He put him to his ears, i.e., confided his secrets to him. Some think he made him a spy over the rest. It is supposed that the meaning of the fable which attributes to Midas very long ears, is, that this king carried the system of espionage to a great length; that he had a multitude of spies in different places.
entries.a98e93f24ba74b1368f20f806766a8e3640a76ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen11378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11379" type="x-p"/> Asahel - was one of the thirty - Asahel was one of those officers, or troops, called the shalishim. This Asahel, brother of Joab, was the same that was killed by Abner, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.23">2Sam 2:23</reference>.
entries.33f9cac0088c8f35776f8156062800ccf66aca54: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen11379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11380" type="x-p"/> Shammah the Harodite - There are several varieties in the names of the following shalishim; which may be seen by comparing these verses with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.27">1Chr 11:27</reference>.
entries.7182e1beaa62f60e7490b0b80e020d06313c99ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen11380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11381" type="x-p"/> Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all - To these the author of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41">1Chr 11:41</reference> adds Zabad son of Ahlai. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.42">1Chr 11:42</reference> - Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.43">1Chr 11:43</reference> - Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.44">1Chr 11:44</reference> - Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.45">1Chr 11:45</reference> - Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.46">1Chr 11:46</reference> - Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.47">1Chr 11:47</reference> - Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite. <div eID="gen11381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11382" type="x-p"/> The 4th and 5th verses are very obscure; L. De Dieu gives them a good meaning, if not the true one: - "The perpetuity of his kingdom David amplifies by a comparison to three natural things, which are very grateful to men, but not constant and stable. For the sun arises and goes down again; the morning may be clear, but clouds afterwards arise; and the tender grass springs up, but afterwards withers. Not so, said he, is my kingdom before God; it is flourishing like all these, but perpetual, for he has made an everlasting covenant with me, though some afflictions have befallen me; and he has not made all my salvation and desire to grow." <div eID="gen11382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11383" type="x-p"/> De Dieu repeats כ ke, the note of similitude, thrice; and the following is his version: - "The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake unto me, (or concerning me): The just man ruleth among men; he ruleth in the fear of God. And, as the sun ariseth with a shining light; as the morning is without clouds by reason of its splendor; as, from rain, the tender grass springeth out of the earth; truly so is not my house with God: because he hath made an everlasting covenant with me; disposed in all things, and well kept and preserved in that order. Although he doth not make all my deliverance and desire to grow, i.e., though some adversities happen to me and my family; yet, that always remains, which, in the covenant of God made with me, is in all things orderly, disposed, and preserved." <div eID="gen11383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11384" type="x-p"/> See Bishop Patrick on the place. <div eID="gen11384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11385" type="x-p"/> Once more I must beg the reader to refer to the First Dissertation of Dr. Kennicott, on the present state of the printed Hebrew text; in which there is not only great light cast on this subject, several corruptions in the Hebrew text being demonstrated, but also many valuable criticisms on different texts in the sacred writings. There are two Dissertations, 2 vols. 8 vo.; and both very valuable.  <chapter eID="2Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen11385" type="x-p"/>

entries.aa6c9eb4170f23ba7b1ff02b7e735acbff03dbe3: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1-2Sam.2.1">2Sa 23:1-2   1</reference>  Divine saying of David the son of Jesse, <div eID="gen4646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4647" type="x-p"/> Divine saying of the man, the highly exalted, <div eID="gen4647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4648" type="x-p"/> Of the anointed of the God of Jacob, <div eID="gen4648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4649" type="x-p"/> And of the lovely one in the songs of praise of Israel.   2  The Spirit of Jehovah speaks through me, <div eID="gen4649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4650" type="x-p"/> And His word is upon my tongue. <div eID="gen4650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4651" type="x-p"/> This introduction to the prophetic announcement rests, both as to form and substance, upon the last sayings of Balaam concerning the future history of Israel (Num 24:3, Num 24:15). This not only shows to what extent David had occupied himself with the utterances of the earlier men of God concerning Israel’s future; but indicates, at the same time, that his own prophetic utterance was intended to be a further expansion of Balaam’s prophecy concerning the Star out of Jacob and the Sceptre out of Israel. Like Balaam, he calls his prophecy a נאם, i.e., a <hi type="italic">divine saying</hi> or oracle, as a revelation which he had received directly from God (see at Num 24:3). But the recipient of this revelation was not, like Balaam the son of Beor, a man with closed eye, whose eyes had been opened by a vision of the Almighty, but “<hi type="italic">the man who was raised up on high</hi>” (על, adverbially “<hi type="italic">above</hi>,” is, strictly speaking, a substantive, “<hi type="italic">height</hi>,” used in an adverbial sense, as in Hos 11:7, and probably also <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:16</reference>), i.e., whom God had lifted up out of humiliation to be the ruler of His people, yea, even to be the head of the nations (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.44">2Sa 22:44</reference>). Luther’s rendering, “who is assured of the Messiah of the God of Jacob,” is based upon the Vulgate, “<hi type="italic">cui constitutum est de Christo Dei Jacob</hi>,” and cannot be grammatically sustained. David was exalted on the one hand as “<hi type="italic">the anointed of the God of Jacob</hi>,” i.e., as the one whom the God of Israel had anointed king over His people, and on the other hand as “the lovely one in Israel’s songs of praise,” i.e., the man whom God had enabled to sing lovely songs of praise in celebration of His grace and glory. זמיר = זמרה does not mean a song generally, but a song of praise in honour of God (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference>), like מזמור in the headings to the psalms. As David on the one hand had firmly established the kingdom of God in an earthly and political respect as the anointed of Jehovah, i.e., as king, so had he on the other, as the composer of Israel’s songs of praise, promoted the spiritual edification of that kingdom. The idea of נאם is explained in 2Sa 23:2. The Spirit of Jehovah speaks through him; his words are the inspiration of God. The preterite דּבּר relates to the divine inspiration which preceded the utterance of the divine saying. בּ דּבּר, literally to speak into a person, as in Hos 1:2. The saying itself commences with 2Sa 23:3.
entries.ae2e6fcfa0286e5b525848b9b9c162fae2da6fe4: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">2Sa 22:3</reference>   <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">3</reference>  The God of Israel saith, <div eID="gen4651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4652" type="x-p"/> The Rock of Israel speaketh to me: <div eID="gen4652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4653" type="x-p"/> A Ruler over men, just, <div eID="gen4653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4654" type="x-p"/> A Ruler in the fear of God.   4  And as light of the morning, when the sun rises, <div eID="gen4654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4655" type="x-p"/> As morning without clouds: <div eID="gen4655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4656" type="x-p"/> From shining out of rain (springeth) green out of the earth.   5  For is not my house thus with God? <div eID="gen4656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4657" type="x-p"/> For He hath made me an everlasting covenant, <div eID="gen4657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4658" type="x-p"/> Provided with all, and attested; <div eID="gen4658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4659" type="x-p"/> For all my salvation and all good pleasure, <div eID="gen4659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4660" type="x-p"/> Should He then not cause it to grow? <div eID="gen4660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4661" type="x-p"/> As the prophets generally preface their saying with “thus saith the Lord,” so David commences his prophetic saying with “<hi type="italic">the God of Israel saith</hi>,” for the purpose of describing it most emphatically as the word of God. He designates God “<hi type="italic">the God</hi>” and “<hi type="italic">The Rock</hi>” (as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">2Sa 22:3</reference>) of Israel, to indicate that the contents of his prophecy relate to the salvation of the people of Israel, and are guaranteed by the unchangeableness of God. The saying which follows bears the impress of a divine oracle even in its enigmatical brevity. The verbs are wanting in the different sentences of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference></hi> and 2Sa 23:4. “<hi type="italic">A ruler over men</hi>,” sc., “will arise,” or there will be. בּאדם does not mean “among men,” but “<hi type="italic">over men;</hi>” for בּ is to be taken as with the verb משׁל, as denoting the object ruled over (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>, etc.). האדם does not mean certain men, but the human race, humanity. This ruler is “<hi type="italic">just</hi>” in the fullest sense of the word, as in the passages founded upon this, viz., <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference>; Zec 9:9, and Psa 72:2. The justice of the ruler is founded in his “<hi type="italic">fear of God</hi>.” אלהים יראת is governed freely by מושׁל. (On the fact itself, see <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>-3.) The meaning is, “A ruler over the human race will arise, a just ruler, and will exercise his dominion in the spirit of the fear of God.”
entries.795d2350e5e724379edb49f80f8afc10fef94a54: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> describes the blessing that will proceed from this ruler. The idea that <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> should be connected with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference></hi> so as to form one period, in the sense of “when one rules justly over men (as I do), it is as when a morning becomes clear,” must be rejected, for the simple reason that it overlooks Nathan’s promise (2 Samuel 7) altogether, and weakens the force of the saying so solemnly introduced as the word of God. The ruler over men whom David sees in spirit, is not any one who rules righteously over men; nor is the seed of David to be regarded as a collective expression indicating a merely ideal personality, but, according to the Chaldee rendering, the Messiah himself, the righteous Shoot whom the Lord would raise up to David (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference>), and who would execute righteousness and judgment upon earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jer 33:15</reference>). <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> is to be taken by itself as containing an independent thought, and the connection between it and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference> must be gathered from the words themselves: the appearance (the rise) of this Ruler will be “<hi type="italic">as light of the morning, when the sun rises</hi>.” At the same time, the Messiah is not to be regarded as the subject to בּקר אור (the light of the morning), as though the ruler over men were compared with the morning light; but the subject compared to the morning light is intentionally left indefinite, according to the view adopted by Luther in his exposition, “In the time of the Messiah it will be like the light of the morning.” We are precluded from regarding the Messiah as the subject, by the fact that the comparison is instituted not with the sun, but with the morning dawn at the rising of the sun, whose vivifying effects upon nature are described in the second clause of the verse. The words שׁמשׁ יזרח are to be taken relatively, as a more distinct definition of the morning light. The clause which follows, “<hi type="italic">morning without clouds</hi>,” is parallel to the foregoing, and describes more fully the nature of the morning. The light of the rising sun on a cloudless morning is an image of the coming salvation. The rising sun awakens the germs of life in the bosom of nature, which had been slumbering through the darkness of the night. “The state of things before the coming of the ruler resembles the darkness of the night” (Hengstenberg). The verb is also wanting in the second hemistich. “<hi type="italic">From the shining from rain</hi> (is, comes) <hi type="italic">fresh green out of the earth</hi>.” נגהּ signifies the brightness of the rising sun; but, so far as the actual meaning is concerned, it relates to the salvation which attends the coming of the righteous ruler. ממּטר is either subordinate to מנּגהּ, or co-ordinate with it. In the former case, we should have to render the passage, “from the shining of the sun which proceeds out of rain,” or “from the shining after rain;” and the allusion would be to a cloudless morning, when the shining of the sun after a night’s rain stimulates the growth of the plants. In the latter case, we should have to render it “from the shining (and) from the rain;” and the reference would be to a cloudless morning, on which the vegetation springs up from the ground through sunshine followed by rain. Grammatically considered, the first view (? the second) is the easier of the two; nevertheless we regard the other (? the first) as the only admissible one, inasmuch as rain is not to be expected when the sun has risen with a cloudless sky. The rays of the sun, as it rises after a night of rain, strengthen the fresh green of the plants. The rain is therefore a figurative representation of blessing generally (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference>), and the green grass which springs up from the earth after the rain is an image of the blessings of the Messianic salvation (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.4">Isa 44:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>). <div eID="gen4661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4662" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference>, Solomon takes these words of David as the basis of his comparison of the effects resulting from the government of the true Prince of peace to the coming down of the rain upon the mown grass.
entries.7b574ee1e37e588f8b6a1fe0467aab014fab30be: <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference> <div eID="gen4662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4663" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>, the prophecy concerning the coming of the just ruler is sustained by being raced back to the original promise in 2 Samuel 7, in which David had received a pledge of this. The first and last clauses of this verse can only be made to yield a meaning in harmony with the context, by being taken interrogatively: “<hi type="italic">for is not my house so with God?</hi>” The question is only indicated by the tone (לא כּי = הלא כּי: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.23">2Sa 19:23</reference>), as is frequently the case, even before clauses commencing with לּא (e.g., Hos 11:5; Mal 2:15 : cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §324, a.). לא־כן (not so) is explained by the following clause, though the כּי which follows is not to be taken in the sense of “<hi type="italic">that</hi>.” Each of the two clauses contains a distinct thought.
